examples.en: On holidays, I go down to my hometown house to see my family.

examples.ko: 고향집은 산 아래에 있는 작은 마을이에요.
examples.en: My hometown house is in a small village at the foot of a mountain.
After a long time, I started missing my hometown house.
At my hometown house, my mother prepared a meal for me.

examples.ko: 방학이 되면 기차를 타고 고향집으로 돌아가요.
examples.en: When vacation comes, I take the train back to my hometown house.
There was a persimmon tree in the yard of my hometown house.

explain: '고향'이 지역을 말한다면 '고향집'은 내가 자랐거나 부모님이 사시는 집을 말해요. 결혼한 사람이 부모님 집을 말할 때는 '본가'라고도 해요. '고향집에 내려가다'처럼 말해요.
explain_en: While '고향' refers to a region, '고향집' refers to the house where you grew up or where your parents live. A married person may also call their parents' house '본가'. You say '고향집에 내려가다' (to go down to the hometown house).

examples.en: Tonight the moon is big and bright too.
The child made a wish to the moon.
Dear moon, please shine on our house too.
The moon is hidden by clouds, so I can't see it.

examples.ko: 할머니가 달님과 토끼 이야기를 해 주셨어요.
examples.en: Grandma told me the story of the moon and the rabbit.
On the full moon, people look at the moon and make wishes.

explain: '달'에 높임 접미사 '-님'을 붙여서 사람처럼 부르는 말이에요. 동화, 동요, 아이에게 말할 때 쓰고 짝말은 '해님'이에요. 일반 설명에서는 그냥 '달'이라고 해요.
explain_en: This is '달' with the honorific suffix '-님', personifying the moon. It is used in fairy tales, songs and when talking to children, and its partner is '해님' (the sun). In ordinary explanations people just say '달'.

examples.en: My child has started learning addition.
We learn addition and subtraction at school.
Addition is easy, but multiplication is hard.
Many children add on their fingers.
The answer to this addition problem is wrong.

examples.ko: 덧셈 문제를 다 풀면 놀러 가도 돼요.
examples.en: Once you finish the addition problems, you can go out to play.

explain: 짝말은 '뺄셈'이고, 곱셈, 나눗셈과 함께 사칙연산이에요. 식을 소리 내어 읽을 때는 '삼 더하기 사는 칠'처럼 '더하기'를 써요. '덧셈'은 사이시옷 때문에 [덛쎔]으로 소리 나요.
explain_en: Its counterpart is '뺄셈', and with 곱셈 and 나눗셈 it makes the four operations. When reading an equation aloud you say '삼 더하기 사는 칠' with '더하기'. Because of the 사이시옷, it sounds like [덛쎔].

examples.en: The hotel room has a small shower stall.
The shower floor is slippery, so be careful.

examples.ko: 운동 후에 헬스장 샤워실을 쓰고 집에 가요.
examples.en: After working out, I use the gym's shower room and go home.
Many people sing in the shower room.
The pool's shower room is narrow but clean.

examples.ko: 샤워실 문이 잘 안 닫혀서 고쳤어요.
examples.en: The shower door wouldn't close properly, so I fixed it.

explain: 한국 집에서는 샤워하는 곳이 보통 화장실 안에 같이 있어서 '화장실'이나 '욕실'이라고 해요. 헬스장이나 수영장처럼 샤워만 하는 공간을 말할 때 '샤워실'을 많이 써요.
explain_en: In Korean homes the shower is usually inside the bathroom, so people say 화장실 or 욕실. 샤워실 is the common word for a space used only for showering, like at a gym or pool.

examples.ko: 저는 밥 먹고 나서 바로 양치질해요.
examples.en: I brush my teeth right after eating.
I was tired yesterday and slept without brushing my teeth.
I brushed my teeth three times today.
Turn off the water while you brush your teeth.
Be sure to brush your teeth before bed.
I took out my toothbrush to brush my teeth.

explain: '양치하다', '이를 닦다'도 같은 뜻으로 써요. 일상에서는 '이 닦았어?'가 가장 자연스러워요. 아이에게는 '이 닦자'라고 말해요.
explain_en: '양치하다' and '이를 닦다' mean the same thing. In daily talk, '이 닦았어?' is the most natural. To a child you say '이 닦자'.

examples.en: I usually go out early in the morning.
It's raining, so I don't want to go out.
My mother has gone out for a moment.
Be sure to take an umbrella when you go out.
On weekends I rest at home and don't go out.
I went out and suddenly got caught in the rain.

explain: '나가다'가 가장 일상적이고, '외출하다'는 볼일이나 놀러 집 밖으로 나가는 일에 써요. 집에 없다는 말은 '외출 중이에요'라고 해요. 윗사람이 나갔을 때는 '외출하셨어요', 돌아오는 건 '돌아오다'나 '귀가하다'예요.
explain_en: '나가다' is the plainest word, and 외출하다 is for heading out of the house to run errands or have fun. 'I'm not home right now' is '외출 중이에요'. For someone senior you say '외출하셨어요', and coming back is '돌아오다' or the more formal '귀가하다'.

en: to depart; to leave a country

examples.en: I leave Korea tomorrow morning.

examples.ko: 출국하려면 비행기가 뜨기 두 시간 전에 공항에 가야 해요.
examples.en: To leave the country, you should get to the airport two hours before the flight.
My friend left the country with his family yesterday.
You can't leave the country without a passport.
I'll text you right after I leave the country.
I'm leaving the country next month to start studying abroad.

explain: 반대말은 '입국하다'예요. 공항에서는 '출국 심사', '출국장'처럼 명사로도 많이 들어요. 보통 '한국을 출국하다'보다 '한국에서 출국하다'나 '출국하다'만 말해요.
explain_en: The opposite is 입국하다 (enter a country). At airports you hear it as a noun a lot: 출국 심사 (departure check), 출국장 (departure hall). People usually say 한국에서 출국하다 or just 출국하다.

dis.h: leave one's country, e.g. by plane

p.n: 출발하다 only says you set off; it does not mean leaving the country.

examples.en: My eyesight is bad, so I wear contact lenses.

examples.ko: 자기 전에 콘택트렌즈를 꼭 빼야 해요.
examples.en: You must take out your contact lenses before going to sleep.
My contact lens fell out of my eye while I was exercising.
Contact lenses are more comfortable than glasses, so I use them often.
My eyes keep getting dry because of my contact lenses.

examples.ko: 새 콘택트렌즈를 사러 안경원에 갈 거예요.
examples.en: I am going to the optical shop to buy new contact lenses.

explain: 일상 대화에서는 줄여서 그냥 '렌즈'라고 많이 말해요. 안경은 '쓰다'지만 렌즈는 '끼다', 뺄 때는 '빼다'를 써요.
explain_en: In daily talk people often shorten it to just '렌즈'. Glasses go with '쓰다', but lenses go with '끼다' (put in), and '빼다' for taking them out.

examples.en: I ate crackers in the car on the way to a trip.

examples.ko: 저는 크래커에 치즈를 올려서 자주 먹어요.
examples.en: I often eat crackers with cheese on top.
These crackers are thin, so they're crispy and nutty.
My child dropped the cracker on the floor and cried.
I ate a bag of crackers as a snack.
Eat the crackers quickly before they go soft.

explain: 한국어에서 '과자'는 봉지에 든 간식 전체를 부르는 말이에요. 크래커는 그중에서 얇고 짭짤한 종류예요. '과자 사 와'라고 하면 크래커뿐 아니라 감자칩이나 쿠키도 다 괜찮아요. '크래커 한 봉지', '크래커 한 상자'처럼 세요.
explain_en: In Korean, 과자 is the general word for packaged snacks, and crackers are one thin, salty kind of it. If someone says '과자 사 와' (buy some snacks), potato chips and cookies are fine too. You count them as '크래커 한 봉지' (a bag) or '크래커 한 상자' (a box).
